folders.name: łódź, poland
folders.description: Łódź developed as a textile center from the 1820s, when authorities designated it a factory settlement. Its population grew from 767 in 1820 to over 314,000 by the end of the 19th century, driven by migration from rural areas and abroad. By 1900, textiles accounted for 94.1% of the city's production, with cotton dominating until the 1880s, when wool's share rose to 37.1%. Large enterprises replaced small workshops: by 1913, 35 factories employed over 500 workers each. The industry collapsed after 1989; the Poltex cotton combine, which had employed over 9,000 people, filed for bankruptcy in 1991.

folders.name: łódź, poland/nowe rokicie, łódź
folders.description: Nowe Rokicie is a former village incorporated into Łódź in stages, with parts annexed in 1906, 1915, and definitively in 1946. It lies in the Górna district and, since 2005, has been an area of the Municipal Information System. Large-scale housing construction began after World War II. The estate was built on 43 hectares with an intended housing density of 45 m² per unit, and its layout concentrated commercial and cultural functions along a north-south axis. By the early 1970s, industrial building technology was used for the final blocks. Four 13-story towers completed around 1962 were the first complex of their kind in the city.

folders.name: łódź, poland/nowe rokicie, łódź/EC-2 combined heat and power plant
folders.description: EC-2 was the first of three thermal power plants built in Łódź after World War II, constructed between 1955 and 1960 at Wróblewskiego street. It began producing heat and electricity on 1 February 1957. The plant initially had eight coal-fired boilers and six turbo-generators, and it was later expanded with two mazut-fired boilers. Its electrical capacity reached 87 MW and thermal capacity 578 MWt. The facility supplied electricity to southern districts of Łódź and Pabianice, and heat primarily to the Retkinia, Karolew, and Czerwony Rynek housing estates. The plant ceased operation on 31 March 2015 after 58 years, due to declining heat demand, worn-out equipment, and new environmental regulations. It was sold by Veolia in 2017 to the Hakamore company, which began demolition. Parts of the complex, including the main building, administrative building, and gatehouse, were entered into the register of monuments, which halted full demolition. The site is now planned for residential development, though preservationists argue the main building should retain its industrial character and be adapted for cultural use. The three flue-gas chimneys at EC-2 — two at 120 metres and one at 160 metres — were unfortunately demolished as part of the site's redevelopment.

folders.name: łódź, poland/nowe rokicie, łódź/EC-2 combined heat and power plant/boiler hall
folders.description: The boiler hall at EC-2 held nine boilers. Four of them were dismantled before the plant was shut down, leaving boilers 5 through 9 in the hall. After the site was bought, the upper floor was demolished, and boiler K-5 was partially dismantled along with it. Boilers K-6, K-7 and K-8 survived in good condition, with only the metal components cut out for scrap missing. Boiler K-9 was dismantled from the top, so it now looks as if it has been cut in half. The boiler hall is one of the best-preserved parts of the entire complex.
